absent: There is nothing on cognitive offloading from before generative AI - no Sparrow, Risko and Gilbert, or Clark and Chalmers - and no educational-philosophical tradition at all: no Dewey, Freire or Barnett, and no decolonial or epistemic-justice sources, even though several of the empirical sites are in Palestine, Indonesia, Vietnam and Ecuador.
forYou: For the AI and Professional Criticality papers this is a useful map of the opposition: the field is arguing about offloading with two-year-old evidence and no epistemology older than the tool, which is precisely the gap your argument about professional judgement can occupy.
method: References from Crossref; strands and narrative by Claude, grounded only in the reference list and title. One duplicated entry in the Crossref list was merged, so 48 of the 49 slots are listed.
narrative:
What stands out in this reference list is how shallow it is in time. Apart from the review machinery - Carroll (2011), Cooke (2012), Aromataris (2020), Campbell (2020), Page (2021), Rethlefsen (2021) and Valizadeh (2022), all borrowed from health-sciences evidence synthesis - almost every source dates from 2024 onwards. The field this paper synthesises has, on its own showing, no memory older than ChatGPT.

Within that thin band two arguments run side by side. One is epistemic: Urban (2025) on metacognitive accuracy, Harkkl (2025) on students' dualistic epistemic practices, Brummernhenrich (2025) on trust cued by politeness, Tomaszewski (2025) on evaluative frameworks, and Pandey (2026) and Susena (2026) on AI as a source of authority. The other is behavioural: Zhang (2024) on AI dependency, Alhur (2025) and Albannai (2025) on reliance, Peters (2025) on assessment integrity, and Pachava (2026) on institutional over-reliance. The review's title promises to hold offloading and autonomy together, and these are the two halves it is trying to join.

The critical-thinking evidence it weighs is mostly very recent and mostly small: Hong (2025), Raitskaya (2025), Waziana (2025), Izquierdo-Condoy (2025), then Balart (2026), Li (2026), Schorr (2026), Chase (2026) and Vendrell (2026). A large share of the underlying studies are language-classroom cases - Thi (2024), Andewi (2025), Pakdel (2025), Al-Atrash (2026), Fujimoto (2026) - which is worth knowing before the conclusions are read as general claims about higher education.
